question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Can small-variant calling from exome or genome sequencing (SNV/indel callers producing MAF rows) ever report a genomic rearrangement whose breakpoints lie in the non-coding region upstream of a gene, or are such events only reported by dedicated structural-variant callers and stored separately? ANSWER: No. SNV/indel callers that produce MAF rows do not report rearrangements, so the teams' assumption is sound: the absence of small-variant rows near a gene is uninformative about rearrangements there. Small-variant callers are size-limited by design (Strelka: 'SNVs and indels up to a predefined maximum size, currently defaulting to 49 bases or less'). The MAF Variant_Type field allows only SNP, DNP, TNP, ONP, INS and DEL; it has no value for a translocation, inversion or breakend. Structural variants are conventionally events of 50 bp or more (deletions, duplications, insertions, inversions, translocations). They are found from different evidence (discordant read pairs, split reads, read depth, local assembly) by dedicated callers such as Manta, Delly, Lumpy, GRIDSS, SvABA and BRASS, which write breakend (BND) records in VCF or BEDPE. The GDC releases these as files separate from the SNV/indel output. The only overlap is at the size boundary: SV callers such as Manta and SvABA also emit medium-sized indels, and a sub-50-bp insertion or deletion in a gene's upstream region could appear as a 5'Flank MAF row if that region was sequenced, but that is a small indel, not a rearrangement joining distant loci. For TERT, a neuroblastoma review states that the rearrangements were discovered by whole-genome sequencing, that breakpoints cluster in a roughly 50 kb region upstream of the TERT transcription start site without affecting the gene itself, and that detection in practice is by FISH or WGS. Exome or targeted capture does not cover that non-coding region, so even an SV caller run on exome data would usually miss them; this last step is an inference from capture design and from sources the department read earlier, not a sentence read in this session. Note: one search also listed primary neuroblastoma TERT-rearrangement studies that may be the source of the task's dataset; they were not opened and nothing from them is used here. HOW SURE: high for the caller and file-format answer; medium for the exome-coverage inference. SOURCES: https://github.com/Illumina/strelka/blob/v2.9.x/docs/userGuide/README.md, https://docs.gdc.cancer.gov/Data/Bioinformatics_Pipelines/DNA_Seq_WGS/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8138798/, https://docs.gdc.cancer.gov/Encyclopedia/pages/Variant_Type/, https://www.ejcped.com/article/S2772-610X(24)00015-1/fulltext.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Pathologist tumour-purity estimates are coarse and unreliable, so adjusting only for the recorded purity field does not rule out a detectability artefact; a VAF-based purity is an accepted complementary check but not an established replacement. Evidence read: (a) Smits 2014: nine pathologists scoring 47 lung slides in bins 0-5, 6-10, 11-20 ... 91-100% differed by 6.3 bins per sample on average, 33% of estimates were >=3 bins from the counted truth, mean absolute error 2.0 bins, and truly <20% samples were called adequate in 38% of observations (overestimation). (b) Mikubo/JTO 2020: pathologists overestimated percent tumour nuclei versus a computational estimate from mutant allele frequencies (used by the sequencing lab as a reference standard); panel assays need >=20-30% tumour content. (c) Haider 2020 (333 prostate tumours, 10 methods): poor concordance between pathology and molecular purity; recommends parameterising genomic analyses with purity estimated from the same analyte being analysed (DNA-derived purity for DNA copy-number work). (d) Counterpoint, Patel 2018 (881 targeted-panel patients): computational purity algorithms agreed poorly with each other, failed often on panel data and did not add value beyond the pathologist estimate; they propose combining mutant allele fraction and copy-number evidence WITH the morphological estimate. NOT SETTLED by the web pages read: the exact recording convention of a clinical panel purity field (step size, floor value, default when unknown) - treat a pile-up at the lowest value as possibly a floor/default code, not a measurement. Practical use (librarian inference, not from sources): run the purity adjustment twice, with recorded purity and with a VAF proxy (e.g. 2 x max or median somatic VAF capped at 1), plus a restriction to samples with clear tumour signal; beware the VAF proxy is biased upward by LOH at the mutated locus (TP53 with 17p loss gives VAF about p/(2-p), not p/2), so exclude TP53 itself from the proxy when comparing TP53 groups. QUESTION: How is pathologist-estimated tumour purity recorded in clinical panel sequencing, how well does it agree with VAF/allele-specific purity, and is a VAF-based estimate a recommended substitute for adjusting copy-number burden? SOURCE: https://www.modernpathology.org/article/S0893-3952(22)01806-3/fulltext ; https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864(19)33409-4/fulltext ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7529507/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6887630/

text: FINDING: The web did not settle this; no source read states that excluding chromosome 17 or 17p is standard when comparing aneuploidy or FGA between TP53-mutant and wild-type tumours, and no source quantified the share of the difference due to chr17. What the pages read do show: the reference pan-cancer aneuploidy score (Taylor 2018) counts altered arms over all arms and reports its correlation with TP53 mutation without any chr17 exclusion appearing in the text retrieved; Donehower 2019 reports that >91% of TP53-mutant cancers lose the second allele, most typically by a 17p deletion, so 17p loss is mechanically coupled to TP53 mutation; a 2025 preprint (Marques et al.) finds p53-deficient tumours have higher aneuploidy pan-cancer but often comparable aneuploidy within a single cancer type, with the consistent difference being more chromosome losses. A targeted search for 'excluding chromosome 17 / 17p' found no paper describing the exclusion as a convention. Background arithmetic (librarian, not from the sources): chr17 is about 81 Mb = ~2.6% of the genome and 17p about 22-25 Mb = ~0.8%, and 17p is 1 arm of 39, so chr17 can contribute at most ~0.026 to FGA or 1-2 arms to an arm count; a group difference much larger than that cannot be explained by chr17 alone. Recommendation: the with-chr17 comparison is the conventional primary analysis, and recomputing FGA/arm score from the .seg file without chr17 (or 17p) is a cheap sensitivity check that should be reported, not a prerequisite. QUESTION: Is it standard to exclude chr17/17p when comparing copy-number burden between TP53-mutant and wild-type tumours, and how much of the difference is attributable to chr17? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6028190/ ; https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(19)30885-X ; https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.07.04.663162

text: FINDING: The web did not identify any published 'aneuploidy score' for panel-sequenced tumours that takes values in the hundreds of thousands to tens of millions; three searches returned only arm-count definitions (Taylor 2018: number of altered arms, 0-39) and arm-fraction definitions, so the provided score's formula remains unknown and must not be assumed. The only continuous copy-number burden family confirmed on a page read is CNApp (broad, focal and global CNA scores computed from segmented log2-ratio data), whose authors state the scores are computed on purity-corrected segments because purity, ploidy and subclonality cause under- or over-estimation of CNAs; i.e. magnitude-based segment scores are purity-dependent unless explicitly corrected. Search snippets (pages not opened, lower reliability) also mention an 'SCNA burden score' defined as the sum of segment log2 ratios normalised by segment length, and a genome-wide score that sums squared per-arm z-scores. Implication (librarian inference): a score on the 1e5-1e7 scale is most likely a length- or marker-weighted sum over segments (for example sum of |seg.mean| x segment length in kb, or total altered length), which would scale continuously with purity-compressed log-ratios and with panel coverage/segmentation, so it is not independent evidence beyond FGA and deserves no more weight than FGA; teams can test candidate formulas against data_cna_hg19.seg (Spearman/ratio of provided score to sum|seg.mean|*length, sum|seg.mean|*num.mark, altered length) and check its correlation with purity and with marker count per sample. QUESTION: Which published 'aneuploidy score' metrics for panel tumours take large continuous values, how are they computed from segments, and do they depend on purity or probe count? label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The convention for declaring a gene 'significantly mutated' in exome discovery screens is a gene-level test against a background (passenger) mutation rate, not a between-tumour-type exact test: either a binomial / likelihood-ratio / CaMP score giving a passenger probability (two-stage discovery + validation/prevalence design), or a MutSig-style burden test. There is no single standard background rate: it is estimated per study (lower/median/upper bounds, from synonymous or non-functional sequence), varies by tumour and nucleotide context, and the CancerMutationAnalysis package default is 0.55e-6 per nucleotide per context; tumour rates span 0.1-100 per Mb. Multiple testing is handled genome-wide by Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (conservative) or empirical-Bayes passenger probabilities (CaMP > 1 targets about 10% false discoveries); large-cohort practice is q <= 0.1. Large studies run each tumour type separately AND the pooled set and report them separately; a gene can be significant pooled but in no single type, or in one type but not pooled, so a pooled result does not show each named type passes. The web gave no convention specific to cohorts under ten tumours per type: methods papers treat such screens as candidate-ranking, to be confirmed in a larger validation/prevalence set (10 discovery + 20 validation tumours: about 59% sensitivity, 58% PPV for major drivers). QUESTION: In small whole-exome discovery cohorts, which test, background rate and multiple-testing correction define 'significantly mutated/associated', and is it per tumour type or pooled? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2820387/ and https://doi.org/10.1214/10-aoas438 and https://rdrr.io/bioc/CancerMutationAnalysis/man/cma.fdr.html and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4048962/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: There is no single universal read-count/depth/allele-fraction threshold for calling a somatic point mutation; it is caller-specific. The rule-based qSNP caller triggers at >=3 reads of the same non-reference allele, >=4 above 20x, and >=5% mutant reads above 50x (2.5% if on both strands); in its orthogonal verification, calls with >=5 mutant reads (>=4 novel starts) were only 57% accurate (98% sensitivity) and >=10 mutant reads were 94% accurate (53% sensitivity), and allele fraction under 10% by itself did not separate true from false calls. MuTect uses a likelihood (LOD) threshold instead of a fixed count and needs >=15x in the normal to avoid germline miscalls. Sensitivity falls steeply with allele fraction and depth: MuTect 95.6% at AF 0.2/30x, 58.9% at AF 0.1/30x, 16% at AF 0.05/30x (51.9% at 60x), 66.4% at AF 0.03/150x; qSNP recovered 68% of verified mutations at 40% tumour purity, 42% at 20% and 15% at 10%. So calls with 2-4 mutant reads sit at or below the usual trigger level and need orthogonal validation to be trusted, and a sample with no call in a gene is 'not detected', not wild-type, unless depth and purity at that gene give adequate power. QUESTION: What minimum mutant reads, depth and allele fraction are conventionally required to call a somatic point mutation in tumour-normal exomes, and how do low cellularity and low depth affect false negatives? text: FINDING: In the cBioPortal mutation file format, Validation_Status, Mutation_Status, n_ref_count and n_alt_count are all Optional columns, so empty values mean 'not recorded', not 'unvalidated' and not 'validated'; an explicit not-validated call would read 'Untested' (allowed values: Valid, Invalid, Untested, Inconclusive, Redacted, Unknown, NA). The empty fields therefore neither support nor weaken the claim that calls were validated. cBioPortal's FAQ states it uses mutation calls as provided by each publication with no additional filtering (only re-annotation through Genome Nexus/VEP) and refers to the publication for callers and filters, so a curated study file is the publication's own call set, and its quality is whatever the publication's filters were. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In clinical targeted-panel tumour sequencing, how is the pathologist-estimated tumour purity field usually recorded (step size, minimum reported value, default when unknown), how well does it agree with purity inferred from somatic variant allele fractions or allele-specific copy-number tools, and is a VAF-based estimate a recommended substitute when adjusting copy-number burden for tumour content? ANSWER: Agreement is poor, so an adjustment that uses only the recorded pathologist purity does not rule out a detectability artefact. A VAF-based purity is an accepted complementary check, but the pages read do not establish it as a replacement. RECORDING CONVENTION: not settled. None of the pages read documents the step size, floor value or unknown-default of a clinical panel purity field. The only related facts are that pathologists score in coarse bins (Smits 2014 used 0-5, 6-10, 11-20 ... 91-100%) and that panel assays ask for at least 20-30% tumour content. A pile-up at the lowest value may therefore be a floor or default code, not a measurement; this is my inference. AGREEMENT: Smits 2014 (nine pathologists, 47 lung slides, counted gold standard): estimates for one slide spanned 6.3 bins on average, 33% were at least 3 bins off, mean absolute error was 2.0 bins, and samples truly below 20% were judged adequate in 38% of observations. Mikubo 2020 (JTO): pathologists overestimated percent tumour nuclei against a computational estimate from mutant allele frequencies, which the sequencing lab used as a reference standard. Haider 2020 (333 prostate tumours, 10 methods): poor concordance between pathology and molecular purity; it recommends parameterising genomic analyses with purity estimated from the same analyte, i.e. DNA-derived purity for copy-number work. COUNTERPOINT: Patel 2018 (881 targeted-panel patients): three computational purity algorithms agreed poorly with each other, often failed on panel data and added no value beyond the pathologist estimate; the authors propose combining mutant allele fraction and copy-number evidence with the morphological estimate. SUGGESTED USE (my inference, not from the sources): repeat the adjustment with a VAF proxy alongside recorded purity, and restrict to samples with clear tumour signal. Leave TP53 out of the proxy, because 17p loss at the mutated locus inflates its VAF and would bias the TP53 group's purity upward. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.modernpathology.org/article/S0893-3952(22)01806-3/fulltext, https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864(19)33409-4/fulltext, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7529507/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6887630/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When comparing genome-wide copy-number burden (fraction of genome altered or arm-level aneuploidy scores) between TP53-mutant and TP53-wild-type tumours, is it standard practice to exclude chromosome 17 or the 17p arm to avoid counting the loss that accompanies TP53 mutation, and how much of the reported difference is typically attributable to chromosome 17? ANSWER: The web did not settle this. No page read states that excluding chr17 or 17p is standard, and none quantifies the share of the TP53-associated difference due to chr17. A targeted search for studies 'excluding chromosome 17 / 17p' returned no paper describing such a convention. WHAT THE PAGES SHOW: Taylor 2018, the reference pan-cancer analysis, defines the aneuploidy score as the count of altered arms over all arms and reports its correlation with TP53 mutation; no chr17 exclusion appears in the text retrieved (only part of the paper was returned, so the methods were not fully checked). Donehower 2019 reports that more than 91% of TP53-mutant cancers lose the second allele, most typically through a 17p deletion, so 17p loss is mechanically coupled to TP53 mutation. The abstract of a 2025 preprint (Marques et al.) says p53-deficient tumours have higher aneuploidy pan-cancer but often comparable aneuploidy within a single cancer type, with more chromosome losses as the consistent difference. SIZE OF THE CHR17 EFFECT (my arithmetic from chromosome sizes, not from the sources): chr17 is about 81 Mb, roughly 2.6% of the genome; 17p is about 22-25 Mb, roughly 0.8%; 17p is one arm of 39. Chr17 can therefore add at most about 0.026 to FGA, or 1-2 arms to an arm count. READING FOR THE TEAMS: the with-chr17 comparison appears to be the usual primary analysis. Recomputing FGA and the arm score from the .seg file without chr17 or 17p is a cheap sensitivity check worth reporting, but nothing read makes it a prerequisite. HOW SURE: low. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6028190/, https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(19)30885-X, https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.07.04.663162.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Which published copy-number summary metrics for panel-sequenced tumours are called an 'aneuploidy score' but take large continuous values (hundreds of thousands to tens of millions) instead of a count of altered chromosome arms, how are they computed from segment data, and do they depend on tumour purity or on the number of probes in the panel? ANSWER: The web did not settle this. Three searches found no published 'aneuploidy score' for panel-sequenced tumours on a 1e5-1e7 scale, so the formula of the provided score remains unknown. Every definition found is an arm count (Taylor 2018: number of altered arms, 0-39; ploidy-adjusted arm-count variants) or an arm fraction. CONFIRMED ON A PAGE READ: CNApp computes continuous broad, focal and global CNA scores from segmented log2-ratio data. Its authors compute them on purity-corrected segments because purity, ploidy and subclonality cause under- or over-estimation of CNAs. Magnitude-based segment scores are therefore purity-dependent unless explicitly corrected. SNIPPETS ONLY (pages not opened or text not retrieved, lower reliability): an 'SCNA burden score' defined as the sum of segment log2 ratios normalised by segment length, and a genome-wide score that sums squared per-arm z-scores. No source read addressed dependence on panel probe count. MY INFERENCE, not from the sources: a score on this scale is most plausibly a length- or marker-weighted sum over segments, for example sum of |seg.mean| x length, or total altered length. Such a score would track purity-compressed log-ratios and panel coverage at least as much as FGA does, so its agreement with FGA is not independent evidence. The teams can test candidate formulas against the .seg file and check the score's correlation with purity and with markers per sample. HOW SURE: low. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7010409/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6028190/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8505672/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In whole-exome discovery screens of small tumour cohorts (fewer than ten tumours per tumour type), how is a gene conventionally declared significantly mutated in, or associated with, a tumour type: which statistical test is used (passenger-probability or background-rate tests versus between-group exact tests), what background mutation rate and what multiple-testing correction are standard, and is the test applied per tumour type or to pooled types? question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In tumour-normal exome sequencing, what minimum number of distinct mutant reads, minimum depth and minimum allele fraction are conventionally required to call a somatic point mutation, and how do low neoplastic cellularity and low depth affect the false-negative rate, so that a sample with no call in a gene can or cannot be treated as wild-type? ANSWER: No single universal threshold exists; it is caller-specific. THRESHOLDS READ: the rule-based qSNP caller triggers a call at a minimum of 3 reads of the same non-reference allele, 4 mutant reads above 20x coverage, and above 50x at least 5% mutant reads (2.5% if on both strands). In its orthogonal verification, requiring 5 mutant reads with at least 4 novel starts gave 57% accuracy at 98% sensitivity, and requiring 10 mutant reads gave 94% accuracy at 53% sensitivity (exomes at about 65x mean coverage). Allele fraction alone discriminated poorly there: under 10% there were 130 true and 112 false calls, over 10% there were 574 true and 422 false. MuTect uses a likelihood (LOD) threshold with filters instead of a fixed read count, and needs at least 15x in the matched normal to keep germline miscalls low. So calls with 2-4 mutant reads sit at or below the usual trigger level and are the class most often false without orthogonal validation; a low allele fraction by itself is not grounds to discard a call. FALSE NEGATIVES: sensitivity falls steeply with allele fraction and depth. MuTect: 95.6% at allele fraction 0.2 and 30x, 58.9% at 0.1 and 30x (53.2% with high-confidence filters), 16.0% at 0.05 and 30x rising to 51.9% at 60x, and 66.4% for 3% allele fraction at 150x. qSNP in tumour/normal mixtures recovered 68% of verified mutations at 40% tumour purity, 42% at 20% and 15% at 10%, and deeper sequencing (>150x) improved but did not restore sensitivity. CONSEQUENCE: a sample with no call in a gene is 'not detected', not wild-type; absence can be asserted only where depth and purity at that gene give adequate power for the expected allele fraction. The pages do not give a 'distinct mutant tags' rule of the kind some discovery screens state in their own methods. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0074380, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3833702/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cBioPortal-format mutation files (MAF), what does it mean when Validation_Status, Mutation_Status, n_ref_count and n_alt_count are empty for every row: are the listed mutations unvalidated, or is validation simply not recorded, and do curated study imports normally contain only mutations that passed the original study's somatic filters? ANSWER: Validation is simply not recorded. The cBioPortal file-format specification lists Validation_Status, Mutation_Status, n_ref_count and n_alt_count as Optional columns. Validation_Status is defined as second-pass results from an orthogonal technology with allowed values Valid, Invalid, Untested, Inconclusive, Redacted, Unknown or NA, so an explicitly unvalidated call would read 'Untested'; an empty cell carries no information either way. The empty fields therefore neither support nor weaken an argument that the calls were validated. Empty n_ref_count/n_alt_count mean normal-sample read counts were not supplied, not that the normal had zero reads. On curation: the cBioPortal FAQ states that it uses the mutation calls as provided by each publication, performs no additional filtering, only re-annotates them through Genome Nexus (VEP, canonical MSKCC transcript), and refers to the publication for the callers and filters used. So a curated study file is the publication's own call set, and whether every row passed somatic filters depends on that publication, not on cBioPortal. Two importer rules apply: rows with Mutation_Status None, LOH or Wildtype are not loaded, and by default Silent, Intron, IGR, 3'UTR, 5'UTR, 3'Flank and 5'Flank rows are filtered out at database load (TERT promoter excepted). That filter runs at load, so a downloaded data_mutations.txt can still contain such rows. For comparison, the legacy TCGA MAF specification requires Mutation_Status = Somatic in a somatic MAF and allows unvalidated somatic calls only in coding regions and splice sites; cBioPortal does not impose that on publication-derived files. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/, https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/, https://docs.gdc.cancer.gov/Encyclopedia/pages/Mutation_Annotation_Format_TCGAv2/.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Standard driver-discovery references define a driver mutation by its effect on the cell that carries it: 'a mutation that directly or indirectly confers a selective growth advantage to the cell in which it occurs' (Vogelstein 2013 glossary), one that 'confers a selective advantage on the cell, increasing survival or proliferation' (Martincorena 2017), and a driver gene as 'one whose mutations increase net cell growth under the specific microenvironmental conditions that exist in the cell in vivo', with mutation patterns in clonal expansions called 'the only way to assess the evidence for a gene being a driver in vivo in humans' (Tokheim 2016). So a positive-selection signature (excess over background, hotspots, dN/dS>1) is read as evidence that the mutations are functional in one specific sense: they raise the fitness (growth/survival) of the clone in its tissue; for blood, Watson 2020 reads selection in sequencing data directly as fitness advantages of haematopoietic clones. It is NOT read as showing which molecular process changes: the same references call statistical hits candidates or 'significantly mutated genes', warn of false positives and no gold standard, and say 'statistics of mutations do not identify' the protein-level change (Nussinov 2019); the splicing and differentiation effects of splicing-factor mutations are attributed in reviews to separate RNA-seq and animal-model work (Saez 2017). No source read states a formal rule that functional data are required before naming a process; that part is inferred from the definitions and from practice (confidence medium). Practical reach: selection evidence can speak against 'no effect on the growth of haematopoietic cells' but cannot by itself show an effect on RNA splicing, and in a small cohort the selection call itself may be a false positive. QUESTION: When a gene or pathway shows a positive-selection signature in somatic mutation data alone, is that treated as evidence of a functional effect on the tissue in which the clone grows, or only as evidence of selection needing separate functional data? label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Purified CD3+ T cells are an accepted and well-performing matched normal for myeloid neoplasms, but 'somatic' then means 'in the tumour fraction and not in the patient's T cells'. Performance: in 16 MDS exomes the marrow-vs-T-cell comparison gave the highest calling rate (197 of 245 validated variants, 80.4%) and missed 1 variant, buccal swabs missed 2, skin biopsy missed 51 (blood contamination); T cells needed >=95% purity and 10 of 26 patients were dropped, partly for >5% myeloid contamination of the T-cell fraction (Padron 2018). Against cultured fibroblasts, T cells had sensitivity 0.91-1.00 and the fewest false positives, while skin and saliva were inconsistent (Jakobsen 2025, 7 patients). Known limit: 'the use of T cells is limited by the presence of evolutionary early somatic mutations like DNMT3A mutations that also are present in the malignant clone' (Blood Cancer J 2017), so a mutation acquired in an early stem cell that also seeded T cells can be subtracted and the patient read as wild-type; a review excerpt (search result only, not opened in full) says DNMT3A clonal-haematopoiesis mutations are found in T cells at lower allele fraction while TET2 mutations appear absent. For splicing genes: SF3B1 mutations in MDS-RS arise in lymphomyeloid stem cells and reach pro-B progenitors, yet show 'little or no' involvement of mature B cells, 'compatible with mutated SF3B1 negatively affecting lymphoid development' (Mortera-Blanco 2017), and mutant stem cells gave myeloid-restricted engraftment in mice (Mian 2015); neither abstract reports T cells directly. Implication: a mutation present in tumour and absent from T cells is acquired and sits in a clone that contributes to myeloid cells but not measurably to the sampled T cells; it does not show origin in a myeloid-committed cell (it may be a stem-cell mutation arising after those long-lived T cells were made, or one whose carriers do not make lymphocytes). This holds for every row of a tumour-vs-T-cell mutation table, so it is a property of the design, not evidence specific to any gene set. Confidence medium: performance data are direct; the lineage reading is inference. QUESTION: What is known about sorted CD3+ T cells versus non-blood tissue as matched normal in myeloid neoplasms, can early stem-cell mutations be in T cells and be filtered out, and what does tumour-present/T-cell-absent imply about lineage? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5969383/ ; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00277-025-06699-y ; https://www.nature.com/articles/bcj201793 ; https://doi.org/10.1182/blood-2017-03-776070 ; https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms10004 ; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41577-023-00843-3 (search excerpt only)

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The myeloid literature's splicing-factor set has a core of four genes, SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2, and a commonly reported extension of PRPF8 and LUC7L2 (Visconte 2019 abstract names exactly these six as 'components of the pre-messenger RNA splicing machinery'), with DDX41 added by Hershberger 2020 ('SF3B1, U2AF1, SRSF2, LUC7L2, PRPF8, DDX41 and ZRSR2 being the most common' of 30+ mutated splicing factors); the original eight-gene set also has SF3A1, SF1, U2AF2 and PRPF40B (seen in search excerpts of two reviews, not in the text returned on opening). LUC7L2 is classed as a splicing factor by most curated sources but is not in the KEGG spliceosome pathway map: the KEGG gene entry hsa:51631 (orthology K13212) has no PATHWAY field and 51631 is absent from the hsa03040 gene list, yet KEGG BRITE places it in 'Spliceosome [BR:hsa03041] > Other splicing related proteins > Spliceosome associated proteins (SAPs) > Other SAPs'. UniProt Q9Y383 GO terms: mRNA splice site recognition (GO:0006376), U1 snRNP (GO:0005685), U2-type prespliceosome (GO:0071004). Daniels 2021 calls LUC7L, LUC7L2 and LUC7L3 paralogs of the yeast U1 snRNA-associated splicing factor Luc7p and 'putative splicing factors', and shows LUC7L2 crosslinks to weak 5' splice sites and the 5' end of U1 snRNA. So including LUC7L2 follows the myeloid-literature and GO convention; excluding it follows a strict KEGG-hsa03040 definition. By Entrez ID (mapping from memory except 51631) the hsa03040 list contains SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, U2AF2, SF3A1, SF1, PRPF40B and PRPF8 but not ZRSR2 (8233) or DDX41 (51428), so a KEGG-pathway-only set would also drop ZRSR2, which every myeloid list includes. Report results under both boundaries. Confidence high for LUC7L2 status, medium for the ID-mapped membership of the other genes. QUESTION: Which genes make up the conventional splicing-machinery gene set in myeloid neoplasms, and is LUC7L2 classed as a spliceosome component or splicing factor in KEGG, GO and the usual myeloid lists? question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cancer genomics, when a gene or pathway shows a positive-selection signature in somatic mutation data alone (mutated far more often than a background model predicts, recurrent hotspot codons, mutual exclusivity among pathway members), how do standard driver-discovery references word what this establishes? Is it treated as evidence that the mutations have a functional effect on the tissue in which the clone grows, or only as evidence of selection that needs separate functional or phenotypic data before any effect on a named biological process can be claimed? ANSWER: Both, at two different levels. (1) What selection is taken to establish: the standard references define a driver by its effect on the carrying cell, so a selection signature is read as evidence of a functional effect in one specific sense - higher fitness (growth/survival) of the clone in its tissue. Vogelstein 2013 glossary: a driver gene mutation is 'a mutation that directly or indirectly confers a selective growth advantage to the cell in which it occurs', a passenger has 'no direct or indirect effect on the selective growth advantage'. Martincorena 2017 (dN/dS): drivers 'confer a selective advantage on the cell, increasing survival or proliferation'. Tokheim 2016: 'A cancer driver gene is defined as one whose mutations increase net cell growth under the specific microenvironmental conditions that exist in the cell in vivo', and evaluating mutations in clonal expansions is 'the only way to assess the evidence for a gene being a driver gene in vivo in humans'. For blood specifically, Watson 2020 reads selection in sequencing data directly as fitness advantages of haematopoietic clones ('positive selection, not drift, is the major force shaping clonal hematopoiesis'). (2) What it is not taken to establish: the molecular process or phenotype through which the advantage arises. The same literature words statistical hits as candidates / 'significantly mutated genes' (Cheng 2016), warns that methods 'yield many false-positive calls' with no gold standard and that 'only a limited number of genes have been fully vetted' (Tokheim 2016), and says 'statistics of mutations do not identify a change in protein conformation' (Nussinov 2019). Reviews attribute the splicing and differentiation effects of splicing-factor mutations to separate RNA-seq and animal-model work, not to mutation statistics (Saez 2017 abstract). Reach for the teams: by field convention a genuine selection signature is admissible indirect evidence against 'no effect on the growth of haematopoietic cells'; it cannot by itself show an effect on RNA splicing, and in a small cohort the selection call may itself be a false positive. Limit of this answer: no source I read states a formal rule that functional data are required before a named process can be claimed; that half is inferred from the definitions and from how the references word their results. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3749880/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5720395/, https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1616440113, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4945827/, https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pcbi.1006658, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6381364/, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aay9333, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5345729/.

FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In somatic mutation calling for myeloid neoplasms, what is known about using sorted CD3+ T cells as the matched normal compared with a non-blood tissue such as buccal cells? Can mutations acquired in an early haematopoietic stem or progenitor cell also be present in T cells and so be filtered out, and what does a mutation found in the tumour fraction but absent from the patient's T cells imply about the lineage in which it arose and expanded? ANSWER: Purified CD3+ T cells are an accepted, well-performing matched normal, but they are blood-derived, so 'somatic' means 'in the tumour fraction and not in the patient's T cells'. Performance: in 16 MDS exomes the marrow-vs-T-cell comparison had the highest calling rate (197 of 245 validated variants, 80.4%) and missed 1 variant; buccal swabs missed 2; skin biopsy missed 51, because of blood contamination. T cells had to be sorted to about 95% purity, and 10 of 26 patients were left out, partly for >5% myeloid contamination of the T-cell fraction (Padron 2018). Against cultured fibroblasts as benchmark, T cells had sensitivity 0.91-1.00 and the lowest false-positive rate, while skin and saliva were inconsistent (Jakobsen 2025, 7 patients). Can early mutations be in T cells and be filtered out: yes. Blood Cancer Journal 2017 states 'the use of T cells is limited by the presence of evolutionary early somatic mutations like DNMT3A mutations that also are present in the malignant clone'. A review excerpt returned by search (the passage was not in the text returned when I opened the page) says DNMT3A clonal-haematopoiesis mutations are detectable in T cells at lower allele fraction than in myeloid cells, while TET2 mutations appear absent from T cells. Residual myeloid cells in the T-cell fraction have the same subtracting effect. So 'wild-type' means 'not detected as tumour-specific relative to T cells', and frequencies are lower bounds. Lineage implication: a mutation in tumour and absent from T cells is acquired and sits in a clone that feeds the myeloid compartment but not, measurably, the sampled T cells. It does not show the mutation arose in a myeloid-committed cell. SF3B1 mutations in MDS-RS trace back to lymphomyeloid stem cells and reach pro-B progenitors, yet show 'little or no' involvement of mature B cells, which the authors call 'compatible with mutated SF3B1 negatively affecting lymphoid development' (Mortera-Blanco 2017); SF3B1-mutant stem cells gave myeloid-restricted engraftment in mice (Mian 2015). Neither abstract reports T cells directly. Because the tumour-vs-T-cell contrast applies to every row of the mutation table, the myeloid-skewed pattern is a property of the design and is not evidence specific to splicing genes. Not confirmed here: the abstract of Shlush 2014 did not load, so the classic report of pre-leukaemic DNMT3A mutations in T cells is not a read source. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5969383/, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00277-025-06699-y, https://www.nature.com/articles/bcj201793, https://doi.org/10.1182/blood-2017-03-776070, https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms10004, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41577-023-00843-3.

FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Which genes make up the conventional 'splicing machinery' or 'spliceosome' gene set used when reporting splicing-factor mutations in myeloid neoplasms, and is LUC7L2 classed as a spliceosome component or splicing factor in standard curated sets (KEGG spliceosome pathway, Gene Ontology mRNA-splicing terms, the usual myeloid splicing-factor lists)? ANSWER: Conventional myeloid set: a core of four genes - SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, ZRSR2 - plus a commonly reported extension of PRPF8 and LUC7L2. Visconte 2019 names exactly these six as mutated 'components of the pre-messenger RNA splicing machinery'; Hershberger 2020 lists 'SF3B1, U2AF1, SRSF2, LUC7L2, PRPF8, DDX41 and ZRSR2' as the most common of 30+ mutated splicing factors. The original eight-gene set also has SF3A1, SF1, U2AF2 and PRPF40B; I saw those four in search excerpts of two reviews (Saez 2017; Visconte 2012 Table 1), not in the text returned on opening the pages. LUC7L2 by source: (a) KEGG pathway map hsa03040 'Spliceosome': NOT a member - the KEGG gene entry hsa:51631 has no PATHWAY field and 51631 is absent from the hsa03040 gene list. (b) KEGG BRITE spliceosome hierarchy br03041: a member, under 'Other splicing related proteins > Spliceosome associated proteins (SAPs) > Other SAPs' (orthology K13212, RNA-binding protein Luc7-like). (c) Gene Ontology via UniProt Q9Y383: mRNA splice site recognition (GO:0006376), U1 snRNP (GO:0005685), U2-type prespliceosome (GO:0071004); UniProt's function line is only 'May bind to RNA via its Arg/Ser-rich domain'. (d) Myeloid literature: counted as a splicing factor; Daniels 2021 describes LUC7L2 as a paralog of the yeast U1 snRNA-associated splicing factor Luc7p, a 'putative' splicing factor that crosslinks to weak 5' splice sites and the 5' end of U1 snRNA and is 'mutated or deleted in myeloid neoplasms'. So including LUC7L2 follows the myeloid-literature and GO convention; excluding it follows a strict KEGG-hsa03040 definition. Both boundaries are defensible and results should be reported under each. Extra caveat: mapping Entrez IDs from memory (only 51631 was confirmed on a page), the hsa03040 list contains SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, U2AF2, SF3A1, SF1, PRPF40B and PRPF8 but not ZRSR2 (8233) or DDX41 (51428), so a KEGG-pathway-only set would also drop ZRSR2, which every myeloid list includes. Confidence is high for LUC7L2's status and medium for the ID-mapped membership of the other genes. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://rest.kegg.jp/get/hsa:51631, https://rest.kegg.jp/link/hsa/hsa03040, https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q9Y383?fields=gene_names,cc_function,go_p,go_c,go_f&format=tsv, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078730/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6966670/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078562/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8394908/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5345729/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3645466/.

The 7 recurrent positions are KRAS G12V (4 MCN: 3/10, 11/30, 18/30, 4/14), KRAS G12D (IPMN_21 7/21, MCN_166 3/6), KRAS G12R (4 IPMN, 83-256 alt), GNAS R201C (4 IPMN, 24-59 alt), CTNNB1 G34R (2 SPN, 18-26 alt), POTEJ R29H (2 MCN, 16 and 49 alt; paralog-family gene) and RNF43 R371* (IPMN_21 2/11, MCN_166 4/15). It cannot be proven real from this file. I carry forward MCN 3/8 as primary (the file is the publication's call set) with 2/8 as the lower bound; IPMN stays 6/8 either way because IPMN_21 also has p.A169T at 81 alt reads. text: REPLY to director Q (per-type background test, bd02-team-b): Poisson background test per type using each tumour's non-silent count, RNF43 CDS 2352 bp (783 codons) over a 30 Mb exome, Bonferroni over 20000 genes. IPMN alone: 6/8 observed vs 0.016 expected, p=2e-14 (Bonferroni 4e-10); stays 6/8 under alt>=8 and truncating filters, 5/8 under both (p=8e-12); still Bonferroni 3e-4 with CDS inflated 10x. MCN alone: full set 3/8 vs 0.009 expected, p=1.1e-7, Bonferroni 0.0023 (0.0077 with a 20 Mb exome, 0.061 with CDS x3, 1 with CDS x10); filtered sets 2/8 give p=3.9e-5, Bonferroni 0.78; truncating and alt>=8 gives 1/8, p=0.009. A truncating-only background test in MCN (13 truncating calls) gives 2 tumours vs 0.001 expected, p=5e-7, Bonferroni 0.01, and RNF43 is the only gene with truncating mutations in >=2 MCNs (also the only one in IPMN, 6 tumours). Recurrence counts (non-silent, of 8 tumours): IPMN 6 genes >=2 and 3 genes >=3 (RNF43 6, KRAS 5, GNAS 5); MCN 5 genes >=2 and 2 genes >=3 (KRAS 6, RNF43 3); SCA 2 and 1 (VHL 4); SPN 1 and 1 (CTNNB1 8). RNF43 is the top gene in IPMN and second in MCN. Rule if each named type must stand alone: the type passes if its own background test survives genome-wide correction on the study's call set and RNF43 is among its top recurrent genes. IPMN passes under every filter; MCN passes on the full call set (and on the truncating test) but not if the 4-read MCN_166 call is discarded. Label stays True under that reading, with MCN resting on that one call; method not changed, the per-type background test is added as a second line of evidence.

MCN by DYSPLASIA: High grade 2/5 mutant (MCN_168, MCN_170), Low grade 1/3 (MCN_166, the 4-read p.R371* call; 0/3 if that call is dropped). IPMN (all 8 High grade) by MAIN_VS_BRANCH_DUCT: Main 4/5, Branch 1/1, Mixed-type 1/2; by HISTOLOGICAL_SUBTYPE: Gastric 2/3, Intestinal 1/1, Oncocytic 1/1, Pancreatobiliary 2/3. The one weak IPMN call (IPMN_21 p.R371*) is in a Main-duct pancreatobiliary tumour that is mutant anyway through p.A169T. No subgroup drives the result, so the compared groups (IPMN+MCN vs SCA+SPN) stay as they are. Scope limits: the IPMN evidence covers high-grade IPMN only, and RNF43 mutation in low-grade MCN rests on a single weakly supported call. Method not changed.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to director Q (comparator sensitivity, bd02-team-b): Per type, calls / median VAF / median depth of all calls: IPMN 214 / 0.32 / 105; MCN 126 / 0.28 / 75.5; SCA 77 / 0.22 / 67; SPN 23 / 0.38 / 60. Per-tumour medians: SCA VAF 0.20-0.39 and depth 40-106, SPN VAF 0.23-0.59 and depth 31-108, MCN VAF 0.19-0.42 and depth 55-148. MCN vs SCA does not differ in per-tumour median VAF (Mann-Whitney p=0.33) or depth (p=0.38); only IPMN is sequenced deeper. Positive control: all 8 SPN carry a CTNNB1 exon-3 mutation with 17-36 alt reads at VAF 0.39-0.59, so SPN sensitivity is good and its low burden (1-7 calls) is biological. SCA: VHL is mutated in only 4/8 (SCA_23, 35, 40 with 12-22 alt reads; SCA_38 with 4 alt reads), so 4 SCAs (14, 27, 29, 37) have no within-type positive control, though each has at least one call with >=22 alt reads and SCA_29 has only 2 calls. The file has no per-gene coverage for unmutated samples, so the 0/16 is 'none detected', firm for SPN and less firm for SCA. Sensitivity: 9/16 vs 0/12 (SPN plus VHL-positive SCA) p=0.0028; vs 0/8 SPN only p=0.0095; the pooled test stays below 0.05 with up to 2 missed comparator mutants (9/16 vs 2/16 p=0.023) and fails at 3 (p=0.066). The per-type background-rate test does not use the comparators at all. Method not changed; the 0/16 is now stated as not detected rather than wild-type.

text: REPLY (bd03-team-b) to director question on chr17: FGA recomputed from the seg file with chr17 removed (|seg.mean|>=0.2) still separates TP53-mut Predominant from the rest: median 0.070 vs 0.0024, Mann-Whitney p=2.2e-11 (with chr17: 0.073 vs 0.0026, p=1e-11); within purity strata <=10 / 11-20 / >20 p=7e-4 / 3e-4 / 0.014; vs each other subtype p<=4e-5; thresholds 0.1 and 0.3 give p=8e-14 and 3e-9; count of non-17 chromosomes with >=50% altered is mean 2.7 vs 0.67 (p=2e-12). chr17 itself is altered over >=50% of its length in 16% of TP53-subtype samples vs 0-2.5% elsewhere, but contributes almost nothing to the genome-wide gap. Changes method: NO; 'increased aneuploidy' is genome-wide, not a 17p artefact.

text: REPLY (bd03-team-b) to director question on a VAF tumour-content proxy: per-sample max VAF from t_alt/(t_alt+t_ref) correlates with recorded purity only moderately (Spearman 0.61) and with FGA 0.65; median max VAF is 0.24 in TP53-mut Predominant vs 0.10 GNAS, 0.10 RAS, 0.125 Triple-Negative, so tumour content does differ by subtype. All 19 samples with no mutation rows are Triple-Negative (median FGA 0.0007, 8 of 19 have FGA exactly 0, 11 have purity 10) and look like low-content samples. (a) Rank regression of FGA-without-chr17 on TP53 subtype adjusted for max VAF: p=1.4e-4 (max VAF incl. TP53), p=2e-8 (max VAF excluding TP53 variants, as the library advised), and p=3e-4 / 4e-7 after also adding recorded purity and histology. (b) Restricted to max VAF>=0.2 (excl. TP53): FGA-no-chr17 median 0.16 (n=48) vs 0.067 (n=40), p=2.5e-4; >=0.3: 0.26 vs 0.10, p=0.002; the opaque ANEUPLOIDY_SCORE is weaker there (p=0.008 at >=0.2, p=0.3 at >=0.3). In the lowest VAF tertile (n=8 TP53) no difference is detectable. Changes method: NO for the label, but the unadjusted gap (about 28-fold in medians) is inflated by tumour content; the content-fair estimate is roughly 2-3-fold higher FGA, and that is how the aneuploidy half should be stated.

text: REPLY (bd03-team-b) to director question on populations: the 29 patients without OS time (27 stage I-III, 1 stage IV, 1 unknown) are 11 TP53-mut Predominant, 10 Triple-Negative, 5 RAS, 3 GNAS, not different from the 244 (chi-square p=0.11; TP53 vs rest Fisher p=0.53). In exactly the 244 survival patients (75 TP53-subtype vs 169) the aneuploidy contrast is unchanged: FGA median 0.068 vs 0.0026 p=7e-11, FGA without chr17 p=1e-10, ANEUPLOIDY_SCORE p=4.5e-11, purity+histology adjusted p=4e-7, and p=0.001 among max-VAF>=0.2 samples; the 29 excluded show the same direction (FGA 0.085 vs 0.002, p=0.04). Changes method: NO; both halves hold in the same 244 stage IV patients, and the prognosis half applies only to stage IV (OS from metastasis).

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd03-team-b) to director question on TP53 vs Triple-Negative survival: comparator rule was written down first (pooled rest; see REPLY-prereg). Triple-Negative (n=66) is 44 goblet cell, 18 mucinous, 4 colonic; purity 10 in 29, 20 in 12, >=30 in 21; 19 of 66 have no detected mutation at all and only 15 have max VAF>=0.2, so it is a mixed group partly made of low-content samples. TP53-subtype vs Triple-Negative OS (131 patients, 61 deaths): unstratified HR 1.30 (0.77-2.19) p=0.33; stratified by histology HR 1.40 (0.77-2.55) p=0.27; with age and grade 1.43 (0.79-2.59); within goblet 1.62, mucinous 1.26, colonic 1.06, all n.s.; against Triple-Negative with max VAF>=0.2 (14 patients, 5 deaths) HR 0.95 (0.34-2.69). TP53 vs pooled rest stays HR 2.35 (1.53-3.62), 2.19 (1.41-3.41) stratified by histology, 2.07 (1.28-3.34) with purity, VAF proxy, grade and age; vs GNAS 2.20 and vs RAS 5.22 stratified by histology (both p<0.02). Changes method or rule: NO; TP53 is never significantly better than any subtype and the pooled effect survives stratification, but the data cannot show TP53-mut is worse than Triple-Negative, so 'poor prognosis' means worse than the cohort and than GNAS/RAS subtypes, sharing the poor end with Triple-Negative.

text: REPLY (bd03-team-b) on the three library findings, checked against the data: (1) chr17: removing chr17 changes the TP53-subtype FGA gap by under 3% (0.070 vs 0.073 median), consistent with the library's bound of 0.026. (2) Purity field: TUMOR_PURITY takes values 5(1),10(123),15(4),20(63),30(38),40(20),50(9),60(7),70(2),80(4),85(1), i.e. 10-point steps with a pile-up at 10 that behaves like a floor; it agrees only moderately with max VAF (Spearman 0.61), so the VAF-proxy adjustment was a needed addition and it did not remove the effect. (3) ANEUPLOIDY_SCORE: none of the tested formulas reproduces it (ratio to sum|seg.mean|xlength, altered length, squared-mean sum is not constant; best Spearman 0.92 with altered-segment |mean|xlength); it correlates with purity 0.53 and not with marker count (-0.05). Its definition stays unknown, so FGA recomputed from the seg file is the primary aneuploidy readout and the provided score is corroboration only. None changes the label.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd03-team-a) to the director's question on TP53 vs Triple-Negative survival. Rule written before the check: 'poor prognosis' is judged on TP53-mut Predominant vs all other subtypes pooled (marginal 'associated with' claim), pairwise contrasts are direction checks. CHECK: Triple-Negative (n=66) is 44 goblet cell, 18 mucinous, 4 colonic; 53/66 poorly differentiated (TP53 subtype: 46 mucinous, 20 goblet, 20 colonic; 40/86 poorly differentiated); purity is 10 for 29/66 and <=20 for 44/66; 19/66 have no mutation rows at all, and all 19 no-mutation samples in the cohort are Triple-Negative (9 goblet, 9 mucinous, 1 colonic). TP53 vs Triple-Negative Cox: unstratified HR 1.30 (0.77-2.19, p=0.33); stratified by histology HR 1.40 (0.77-2.55, p=0.27); stratified by differentiation HR 1.59 (0.92-2.77, p=0.10); within goblet HR 1.62, within mucinous HR 1.26, within colonic HR 1.06 (all HR>1, none significant; 61 deaths). TP53 vs pooled rest stratified by histology HR 2.19 (1.41-3.41, p=5e-4); excluding the 19 no-mutation samples HR 2.43 (1.56-3.78). FINDING: the TP53 subtype is never better than Triple-Negative, the direction is the same in every histology stratum, but TP53 and Triple-Negative (a goblet-cell, poorly differentiated group) are statistically indistinguishable and share the poor-prognosis end. Changes method or rule: NO; the pooled contrast stays primary and stays significant with histology held fixed. Wording change: 'worse than GNAS and RAS subtypes, similar to Triple-Negative'.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd03-team-a) to the director's question on a VAF tumour-content proxy. CHECK: per-sample highest VAF = t_alt/(t_alt+t_ref) from data_mutations.txt (1084 somatic rows, 254 samples), also computed leaving out TP53 and leaving out all chr17 genes. All 19 samples with no mutation rows are Triple-Negative (FGA median 0.0007, max 0.10, 8 with FGA exactly 0, 3 with any altered arm, purity median 10) - so they are low-signal comparator samples; dropping them leaves FGA 0.073 vs 0.003, p=8e-11. Proxy vs recorded purity Spearman 0.61-0.63; proxy vs FGA 0.61-0.65; proxy is higher in TP53 subtype (median max-VAF excluding TP53 0.22 vs 0.10-0.125 in others, p=1e-9), so tumour content is a real confounder. (a) Rank regression of each aneuploidy metric on TP53-subtype + proxy rank: TP53 coefficient stays positive on all 5 metrics - with the TP53-excluded proxy coef 0.14-0.15 rank units, p<=4e-5 (n=251); with the raw max VAF (biased against TP53 by 17p LOH) coef 0.08-0.11, p<=0.012; unchanged when recorded purity is added. (b) Restriction: proxy(no TP53)>=0.2: FGA median 0.159 (n=48) vs 0.066 (n=40), p=1.7e-4, altered arms excluding chr17 6 vs 2, p=9e-5; proxy>=0.3: FGA 0.262 (n=24) vs 0.100 (n=19), p=0.0015; proxy>=0.2 AND purity>=20: 0.156 vs 0.065, p=6e-4. Within proxy tertiles: high p=6e-4, mid p=0.004, low p=0.15 (only 8 TP53 samples, same direction). FINDING: about half of the raw gap is attributable to tumour content (unadjusted rank coefficient about 0.25 falls to about 0.14), but the TP53 subtype has roughly 2.4-2.6 times the FGA of the rest even among samples with clear tumour signal. Changes method: NO. I state the aneuploidy half as 'higher, with the gap partly but not wholly explained by tumour content'.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd03-team-a) to the director's question on ECOG, PCI and treatment variables. CHECK among the 244 patients with OS (84 deaths): ECOG vs subtype chi2 p=0.28 (ECOG 'Unknown' for 51: 12 GNAS, 9 RAS, 17 TP53, 13 TN); CRS_NUMBER differs (p=6e-4): no cytoreductive surgery in 28/75 TP53 (37%) vs 24/169 rest (14%); IPCHEMO_FIRST_CRS yes in 16/75 TP53 vs 77/167 rest (p=0.008); FIRSTLINE_CHEMO_GROUP differs (p=0.001) mainly through missing/no chemo (22/78 GNAS vs 2/75 TP53); PCI is missing for 123/244 (54/75 TP53 = 72%, vs 36/78 GNAS, 11/35 RAS, 22/56 TN), missing almost always when CRS_NUMBER=0 (49 of 52), median PCI 12 in TP53 vs 21 GNAS, 11.5 RAS, 16.5 TN. Cox for TP53 subtype vs rest: unadjusted HR 2.35 (1.53-3.62); +ECOG>=1 HR 2.05 (1.25-3.35, n=193); +any CRS HR 1.99 (1.29-3.09); +ECOG+any CRS HR 1.88 (1.15-3.08, p=0.012, 67 deaths, 3 coefficients); ECOG with Unknown as a category + any CRS on all 244: HR 1.73 (1.09-2.73, p=0.019); +ECOG+CRS+poor differentiation+age HR 1.89 (1.14-3.13); 8-coefficient model HR 1.75 (1.04-2.95, p=0.035); stratified by ECOG x any-CRS HR 1.68 (1.06-2.67); within no-CRS HR 2.52 (1.17-5.40), within CRS HR 1.60 (0.90-2.82). PCI complete cases (n=121, 34 deaths): HR 2.52 (1.11-5.71) adjusted for PCI; PCI+ECOG+poor (n=91, 29 deaths) HR 1.70 (0.67-4.30), underpowered. FINDING: TP53-subtype patients less often had surgery, which explains part of the excess hazard (HR 2.35 -> about 1.7-2.0), but the hazard ratio stays above 1 and significant in every model within the events limit; CRS is a post-baseline variable (also a marker of resectability, possibly a mediator), and PCI is too missing in the TP53 group to adjust for reliably. Changes method: NO; the marginal contrast stays primary; I describe prognosis as 'worse OS, partly but not fully accounted for by performance status and less surgery; PCI-adjusted result uninformative'.

text: REPLY (bd03-team-a) to the director's question on chromosome 17. CHECK: recomputed FGA and arm calls from data_cna_hg19.seg (|seg.mean|>0.2, arm altered if >=70% of covered length in one direction) with chr17 removed (37 autosomal arms). 17p loss is called in 16/86 TP53-subtype samples vs 3/187 rest, 17q loss in 12/86 vs 0/187, so chr17 is indeed enriched. Without chr17: FGA median 0.061 [0.006-0.193] vs 0.002 [0-0.024], p=9e-11, AUC 0.744 (with chr17: 0.067 vs 0.002, p=4e-11, AUC 0.748); altered arms median 2.5 [0-7] vs 0 [0-0], mean 4.06 vs 0.85, p=2e-14 (with chr17: median 3, mean 4.38 vs 0.87); >=1 altered non-chr17 arm 58/86 vs 42/187 (OR 7.2, p=1e-12, identical to with-chr17); >=3 altered non-chr17 arms 43/86 vs 24/187 (OR 6.8). Both losses (median 1 vs 0, p=7e-14) and gains (1 vs 0, p=2e-11) outside chr17 are higher. At threshold 0.1: 9 vs 1 arms. TP53 stays higher than each other subtype without chr17 (FGA p<=9e-5, arms p<=5e-6). FINDING: chr17 contributes on average 0.32 of the 4.38 altered arms per TP53-subtype sample (0.02 in the rest); the difference rests on about 3 extra altered arms per sample genome-wide, not on the defining locus. Changes method or reading: NO.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd03-team-a) on the library findings. (1) Aneuploidy-score formula: tested candidates from the .seg file against ANEUPLOIDY_SCORE - altered length (|seg.mean|>0.2) Spearman 0.91, sum of |seg.mean| x length over altered segments Spearman 0.92, but Pearson only 0.67 and ratios not constant, so no candidate reproduces it; formula stays unknown. The score correlates with purity (rho 0.53) and not with markers per sample (rho -0.05; median markers 7708 in both groups), and the FGA difference holds within each panel version (IM5: 0.066 vs 0.006, p=1e-5; IM6: 0.081 vs 0.002, p=5e-7). I treat the provided score as a purity-dependent correlate of FGA, not independent evidence; the conclusion rests on FGA plus the recomputed arm count with tumour-content adjustment. (2) Purity field: confirmed coarse (10 for 123/273); followed the suggestion to use a max-VAF proxy excluding TP53 - result in the VAF REPLY. (3) chr17 exclusion run as a sensitivity check - result in the chr17 REPLY. None changes the method or the label (True).

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd02-team-a) to the director's question on a constant-free recurrence check: Counting genes with a protein-altering mutation per tumour type (8 tumours each), on the full call set IPMN has 179 mutated genes, 6 in >=2 tumours and 3 in >=3 (RNF43 6/8 rank 1, KRAS 5, GNAS 5); MCN has 100 mutated genes, 5 in >=2 (KRAS 6, RNF43 3, MUC4 2, POTEJ 2, TP53 2) and 2 in >=3, RNF43 rank 2; SCA has only VHL (4/8) and SPN only CTNNB1 (8/8) and RNF43 is absent. Keeping only calls with >=5 mutant reads (also with depth>=10 or allele fraction>=0.05): IPMN unchanged (RNF43 6/8 rank 1); MCN has no gene in >=3 and five tied at 2/8 (RNF43, KRAS, TP53, MUC4, POTEJ), because the filter removes 4 of the 6 MCN KRAS codon-12/13 hotspot calls as well as one RNF43 call. RNF43 is the only gene in the file with truncating mutations in >=2 tumours of one type (IPMN 6, MCN 2 on the full set; IPMN 5, MCN 1 with >=5 reads). Using only the 350 genes mutated anywhere in the file as the gene universe (no outside constants, far too small so conservative), Poisson-binomial P(a named gene hit in >=6/8 IPMN)=1.8e-6 (x350=0.0006), P(>=3/8 MCN)=0.0027 (x350=0.93), P(>=2/8 MCN)=0.028-0.036. RULE when each named type must stand alone: a type passes if RNF43 is protein-altered in >=2 of its tumours at distinct sites and the gene-level tail probability is <0.05, judged as a test of the one named gene (the hypothesis names RNF43) and also reported after all-gene correction; state the result on the study call set and on the >=5-read set. IPMN passes every version. MCN passes on the call set (3/8: named-gene p=0.0027 with no constants, 3e-4 after x20,000) and on the >=5-read set only as a named-gene test (2/8: p=0.028; all-gene correction gives 0.2). This does not change the method or the label (True); it makes the MCN arm explicitly conditional on the 4-read call or on the named-gene reading.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd02-team-a) to the director's question on weak RNF43 calls: Within-tumour ranks (from lowest). MCN_166 RNF43 p.R371* has 4 mutant reads of 15: alt count rank 2 of 28 (six other calls in that tumour also have 4, and its KRAS G12D has 3 of 6), depth rank 2 of 28, allele fraction 0.27 rank 11 of 28 (tumour median 0.38), so the allele fraction is ordinary and only depth is low. MCN_170 p.S41* has 14 mutant reads of 194: alt rank 5 of 12, depth rank 8 of 12, allele fraction 0.072 is the lowest in the tumour and the lowest of all 440 calls in the file, so it is well supported by reads but subclonal; my earlier text wrongly called it low read support. IPMN_21 p.R371* has 2 of 11 reads, the lowest alt count and depth of its 28 calls and lowest allele fraction (0.18), but that tumour also has RNF43 p.A169T at 81 of 196 reads so its status does not depend on the weak call. The 7 positions called in more than one sample: KRAS G12V (4 MCN; 3/10, 11/30, 18/30, 4/14), KRAS G12D (IPMN_21 7/21, MCN_166 3/6), KRAS G12R (4 IPMN, 83-256 reads), GNAS R201C (4 IPMN, 24-59 reads), CTNNB1 G34R (2 SPN, 18 and 26 reads), POTEJ R29H (2 MCN, 16/110 and 49/218, each with a second POTEJ variant within 35 bp, a paralog-artefact pattern) and RNF43 R371* (IPMN_21 2/11, MCN_166 4/15). Five of seven are driver hotspots; RNF43 R371* has the lowest read support of the seven but resembles the MCN KRAS hotspot calls (3-4 reads at depth 6-14), not the POTEJ pattern. Because a >=5-read filter would also discard 4 of 6 MCN KRAS hotspot calls that are clearly real, low-read calls in this curated set cannot be treated as false. I carry forward MCN 3/8 as the primary count and 2/8 (MCN_168, MCN_170) as the strict lower bound, not 1/8. Method unchanged; the sensitivity bound for MCN is corrected from 1/8 to 2/8.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd02-team-a) to the director's question on comparator wild-type calls: Per type, all calls: IPMN 214 calls (7-42 per tumour), median allele fraction 0.32, median depth 105; MCN 126 (8-28), 0.28, 76; SCA 77 (2-17), 0.22, 67; SPN 23 (1-7), 0.38, 60. Allele fraction differs by type (Kruskal-Wallis p=1.6e-9); SCA is lower, SPN is higher. Every one of the 8 SPN tumours has a CTNNB1 exon-3 call with 17-36 mutant reads and allele fraction 0.39-0.59, so SPN tumours have high neoplastic content and their lack of RNF43 calls is reliable despite few calls. In SCA the most recurrent gene is VHL in only 4 of 8 (21-22 reads in two, 12 and 4 reads in the others); SCA_14, SCA_27, SCA_29 and SCA_37 have no VHL call, and SCA_29 has only 2 calls, so SCA absences are 'not detected' rather than proven wild-type, though SCA still yields calls down to 4 reads and 11% allele fraction. The file has no per-sample coverage of RNF43, so depth at RNF43 in unmutated tumours cannot be checked. Effect on the between-group test: pooled IPMN+MCN 9/16 vs SPN only 0/8 Fisher p=0.0095, vs SPN plus VHL-positive SCA 0/12 p=0.0028, vs all 0/16 p=0.0008; IPMN 6/8 vs SPN 0/8 p=0.007; MCN 3/8 vs SPN 0/8 p=0.2. The pooled result stays below 0.05 if up to 2 comparator tumours hid a missed mutation (p=0.023) and is lost at 3 (p=0.066). So the comparators remain usable, the pooled and IPMN between-group results hold on the reliable comparator alone, and the MCN-alone between-group result does not. Method unchanged; the between-group result is stated less firmly and the MCN arm rests on the gene-level reading.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd02-team-a) to the director's question on DYSPLASIA, duct type and histological subtype: MCN by dysplasia, any RNF43 call: High grade 2 of 5 (MCN_168 p.R127P 38 reads, MCN_170 p.S41* 14 reads), Low grade 1 of 3 (MCN_166 p.R371*, 4 of 15 reads), Fisher p=1.0; counting only calls with >=5 mutant reads: High grade 2 of 5, Low grade 0 of 3, p=0.46. IPMN: all 8 are High grade, RNF43 mutated in 6. By duct type: Main 4 of 5, Branch 1 of 1, Mixed-type 1 of 2. By histological subtype: Gastric 2 of 3, Pancreatobiliary 2 of 3, Intestinal 1 of 1, Oncocytic 1 of 1. The only weak IPMN call (IPMN_21 p.R371*, 2 of 11 reads) sits in a Main-duct pancreatobiliary tumour that also carries a strong RNF43 call. RNF43 mutation is spread across every duct type and subtype of IPMN and across both grades of MCN, not confined to one subgroup, so the comparison group does not change. Scope: the IPMN evidence covers high-grade IPMN only, and well-supported MCN mutations are seen only in high-grade MCN (numbers too small to test). Method and label unchanged.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd02-team-a) on the three library findings, checked against the data: (1) Validation_Status, Mutation_Status, n_ref_count and n_alt_count are empty in all 440 rows, so validation cannot be read from the file; internal evidence that low-read calls are real is that 4 of 6 MCN KRAS codon-12/13 hotspot calls have only 3-4 mutant reads. The file keeps 37 non-coding or silent rows (Intron 14, Splice_Region 10, RNA 7, UTR/Flank 5, Silent 1), none in RNF43. (2) Read thresholds: 35 of 440 calls have <5 mutant reads and 4 have <=3; RNF43 calls with <5 reads are MCN_166 (4/15) and IPMN_21 second hit (2/11); MCN_170 has 14 reads at 7% allele fraction and is kept under a read-count rule. Absence of a call is 'not detected': reliable for SPN (clonal CTNNB1 in 8 of 8), weaker for SCA. (3) Gene-level background test per type is the convention; a pooled result does not prove each type. Per type: IPMN passes genome-wide; MCN passes on the call set (3/8) and, with >=5 reads (2/8), only as a named-gene test. Label stays True.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd01-team-a) to the director's question on TMB versus mutation-file rows: confirmed. TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS x 30 equals the row count for 28 of 29 samples; tAML-01 has TMB 0.5 (=15) but 14 rows, so the sample table implies 261 mutations against 260 rows. I also found something I had missed: 9 same-sample same-site pairs (18 rows; BCOR, KBTBD4, KRT14, LTBP2, MCRS1, PHF8, ROCK2, SORBS2, UBE2Q1) that look like one event written two ways, so independent events are about 251. None of these rows, and no plausible identity for the one missing row, changes the enrichment: with N=251, 260 or 261 the expected number of hits in the pre-fixed 8-gene splicing set is 0.13 versus 16 observed (Poisson p ~3e-28; ~1e-12 with a 10x mutability allowance), and the set would need to be about 4 percent of the exome (~1.2 Mb, 80x its real size) before 16 hits became unremarkable. The gene lengths taken from memory were checked against UniProt and all are exact. Does not change the method; N should be reported as 251-261.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd01-team-a) to the director's question on splice-site-class variants in splicing genes: confirmed. Of the 11 Splice_Site rows, two are in splicing-related genes: ZRSR2 c.771+1G>A in MDS-06 (already counted as exposure by gene symbol) and LUC7L2 c.156+2dup in CMML-01, who also carries U2AF1 Q157R. LUC7L2 was not in my pre-fixed list (8 genes plus KEGG hsa03040); the library confirms it is outside KEGG hsa03040 but inside the myeloid-literature and GO splicing sets. Including it: carriers stay 16/29 (8-gene set) or 14/29 (4-gene core), but one patient now has two splicing genes hit, and the exclusivity permutation p moves from 0.013 (8-gene set, 0 overlaps) to 0.05 (4-gene core), 0.07 (8 genes + LUC7L2) and 0.20 (core4 + PRPF8 + LUC7L2). The exclusivity result therefore depends on the gene list, so by my own pre-stated rule it changes the method: mutual exclusivity is dropped as supporting evidence and reported as descriptive only ('exactly one gene per patient' is true only for the list without LUC7L2). The enrichment (p<1e-10 under every list, with 10x allowance) and the hotspot pattern do not depend on LUC7L2.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd01-team-a) to the director's question on disease type as a three-category table: confirmed that the result depends on the gene set. Carriers by AML/CMML/MDS (n=7/4/18): 4-gene core (SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, ZRSR2) 1/4/9, Freeman-Halton exact p=0.021; pre-fixed 8-gene set 2/4/10, p=0.104; adding LUC7L2 changes neither table because its only carrier already has U2AF1. Per gene no table is below p=0.10 (U2AF1 0/2/3 p=0.10; ZRSR2 1/1/3 p=1.0; SRSF2 0/1/2 p=0.48). The whole signal is CMML 4/4 (four patients) and the two extra AML carriers that the 8-gene set adds (SF3A1, PRPF40B single missense variants). With 29 patients, a subset effect driven by 4 cases and a p-value that crosses 0.05 by changing the list, the disease-type pattern can carry essentially no weight for the haematopoiesis half, and it is a within-disease subtype association, not an effect on haematopoiesis. Does not change my method: I had not used disease type as support; the answer now says explicitly that it is set-dependent and not used.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd01-team-a) to the director's question on the label rule. Splicing half: exposure = splicing-gene rows of data_mutations.txt (Hugo_Symbol, Variant_Classification, HGVSp_Short, Protein_position); outcome = none (no RNA, expression or isoform table; Splice_Site/splice_region annotations are predicted cis consequences for the mutated gene's own transcript, not measurements). Alone, this half is Not verifiable. Haematopoiesis half: same exposure; no direct outcome (no blood counts, blasts, dysplasia); proxies = ONCOTREE_CODE/CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED, WHO_CLASS, CYTOGENETICS, IPSS_SCORE, plus the sampling design (every call is a clonal variant in a bone-marrow haematopoietic clone relative to germline control), which lets a selection test speak to the fitness of haematopoietic clones. The hypothesis is one joint claim ('affects neither splicing nor haematopoiesis'): it can be supported only if both halves are, but is contradicted if either half is, so evidence on the haematopoiesis half alone can give 'False' and nothing in these tables could give 'True'. The task's definitions say 'relevant variables' and give as the Not-verifiable example a variable that is wholly absent; they do not say the outcome must be directly measured. My rule: False if pre-specified indirect evidence (enrichment over background plus hotspot/truncating pattern) contradicts no-effect on haematopoiesis; Not verifiable if a direct readout is required. The check (enrichment p<1e-10 under every gene set and every N, recurrent SRSF2 P95 and U2AF1 Q157 codons) meets the first rule. Does not change my method or label (False); this reading of the label definition remains the weakest point, and under the strict reading the label would be Not verifiable.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd01-team-a) on the three library findings, each checked against the data. (1) T-cell normal: 27/29 controls are CD3+ T cells and both buccal-control patients (MDS-10, tAML-07) have no splicing-gene call, so frequencies are lower bounds and 'present in marrow, absent in T cells' applies to every row; I therefore do not use lineage restriction as evidence, only enrichment over the cohort's own background. (2) Splicing gene set: LUC7L2 is the only extra myeloid-list gene in the file (one splice-donor variant, CMML-01, co-occurring with U2AF1 Q157R); PRPF8 and DDX41 have no rows; results are now reported under both boundaries and the exclusivity leg, which depends on the boundary, is dropped. (3) Driver convention: the selection signature is used only as indirect evidence of a fitness effect on haematopoietic clones, not of any splicing change; the small-cohort false-positive risk is low here because the enrichment holds at p<1e-10 with a 10x mutability allowance, with any one gene removed, and with N from 251 to 261.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to director question on matched-normal tissue (bd01-team-b): GERMLINE_CONTROL is CD3+ T cell for 27 of 29 patients and buccal mucosa for 2 (MDS-10, tAML-07); tumour is bone marrow in 27 and CD3-negative peripheral blood in 2. So a somatic call means 'present in marrow/CD3- cells and absent from the patient's own T cells' for 27 patients: every one of the 17 splicing-gene rows comes from a T-cell-control patient, so those mutations are in the non-T (myeloid) compartment, and 'no mutation detected' can be a false negative if an early mutation is also carried by T cells. This filter applies equally to all 260 rows (passengers included), allele counts are empty (0 of 260 filled) so clone size cannot be estimated, and splicing carriers are 0/2 with buccal control vs 16/27 with T-cell control (Fisher p=0.19). It is a caveat on reading negatives, not a haematopoiesis outcome that differs by splicing-mutation status. Changes method: no.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to director question on label rule per half (bd01-team-b): I re-read the three label definitions; they ask for 'relevant variables', not literally a directly measured outcome, and the hypothesis is a joint claim, so evidence against either half would make it False. Half 1 RNA splicing: exposure = Hugo_Symbol/variant columns of data_mutations.txt; outcome or proxy columns = none (no expression, exon-usage or transcript table; Splice_Site in Variant_Classification is a variant type, not a splicing readout). Half 2 haematopoiesis: exposure the same; proxies = WHO_CLASS, ONCOTREE_CODE/disease type, IPSS_SCORE (13 of 29), CYTOGENETICS; no blood counts, blast percent, or controls, and every patient has a myeloid neoplasm so disease presence does not vary. My rule was applied to each half: half 1 has no variable; half 2 proxies were tested and gave no robust association (pre-fixed 8-gene list, 3-group disease permutation p=0.09; IPSS p=0.76). The only robust signal is enrichment/hotspot recurrence, which uses the exposure column plus a background model and is an inference about selection, not an outcome variable. Changes method: no; label stays Not verifiable, with False as the alternative if selection evidence is accepted as evidence about haematopoiesis.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to director question on the sex-chromosome gene (bd01-team-b): ZRSR2 is on chrX and all 5 ZRSR2 mutations are in males (0/10 females, 5/19 males). The pooled sex association of splicing-mutation status (pre-fixed 8-gene list: females 3/10, males 13/19, Fisher p=0.064) is carried by ZRSR2: without ZRSR2 it is females 3/10, males 8/19, p=0.69. The disease-type association is not carried by ZRSR2 or by sex make-up (sex is balanced across groups: CMML 1F/3M, MDS 7F/11M, tAML 2F/5M; ZRSR2 alone by disease p=1.0) but it is not robust either: pooled p=0.09, without ZRSR2 p=0.13, without SRSF2 p=0.42, without U2AF1 p=0.76, males only p=0.15, and no single gene is significant (U2AF1 CMML 2/4 vs MDS 3/18 vs tAML 0/7, p=0.15). Changes method: no; it confirms that no pooled clinical association should be used as evidence of an effect.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to director question on pre-fixed gene list and strict variants (bd01-team-b): the 8-gene list U2AF1, SRSF2, SF3B1, ZRSR2, SF3A1, SF1, U2AF2, PRPF40B was written in my PLAN before the mutation file was opened; the 3-gene set (U2AF1, SRSF2, ZRSR2) was post hoc and is dropped. Pre-fixed list, all variants: 16/29 carriers, 16 hits in 16 patients, exclusivity permutation p=0.013, disease-type p=0.09. Core-4 list: 14/29, exclusivity p=0.05, disease p=0.022. Strict functional variants only (codon hit in >=2 patients, or truncating: SRSF2 P95 x3, U2AF1 Q157 x3, ZRSR2 truncating x3): 9/29 carriers, exclusivity p=0.34, disease-type p=0.13. Enrichment over a CDS-length background survives everything: leave-one-gene-out p<=2.4e-8 even at 10x background, strict-only 9 hits p=3.5e-6 at 10x background (worst leave-one-out 1e-3). So carrier count is 9 to 16 depending on definition; exclusivity and disease-type results are not robust; only enrichment/hotspot recurrence is. Changes method: no change of label rule; I now report the pre-fixed list as primary and no longer cite exclusivity or disease type as support.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to library finding on the splicing gene set and LUC7L2 (bd01-team-b), checked against the data: of the library's genes, the mutation file has U2AF1 5, ZRSR2 5, SRSF2 3, SF3B1 1, SF3A1 1, PRPF40B 1, LUC7L2 1 (splice site, in CMML-01 who also has U2AF1 Q157R); PRPF8, DDX41, SF1 and U2AF2 have zero rows. Including LUC7L2 does not change the carrier count (16/29 with the 8-gene list, 14/29 with core-4 either way) but breaks perfect exclusivity (8-gene+LUC7L2: 17 hits in 16 patients, p=0.058; core-4+PRPF8+LUC7L2: 15 hits in 14 patients, p=0.17). Disease-type p is 0.02 to 0.09 across boundaries. The gene-set boundary therefore changes the exclusivity result but not the enrichment result or the label. Changes method: no.

label: REFEREE TEST
text: Task bd01 (hypothesis: splicing-machinery mutations do not affect RNA splicing or haematopoiesis; 29 myeloid-neoplasm exomes, 260 somatic rows, no RNA or blood-count table): teams X (Not verifiable) and Y (False) agreed on all numbers and differed only on whether recurrence/selection evidence counts. Referee test calibrated the recurrence readout inside the mutation table: only 11 of 224 genes are hit in 2+ patients, and they are 3 splicing genes (U2AF1 5, ZRSR2 5, SRSF2 3), 7 known haematopoietic drivers (TET2 8, NRAS 3, TP53, EZH2, DNMT3A, ASXL1, KRAS) and BCOR; the 8-gene splicing set hits 16/29 patients, equal to a 14-gene known-driver positive control (16/29), versus a maximum of 9 for 100,000 random 8-gene sets from other genes in the file; the only codons hit in 3 patients are U2AF1 Q157 and SRSF2 P95. Outcome supported Y, so the referee picked False; the RNA-splicing half is unmeasured in the data.
